title: Inupiaq postbase tool
Taiguaqta by Edna Ahgeak MacLean
text:
Inupiaq





  
  
    
    
       Nukatpiaġruk   niksiksuqtuq.


      
          Nukatpiaġruk   niksiksuq-tuq
        
          boy.before.puberty   to.fish-statement.he
        
         The word “nukatpiaġruk” means a young boy. This is the doer of our sentence’s action.
        
         This next word is our verb base. “niksIksuq” means to fish, but this verb also needs to tell us who is doing fishing.
        
         To show who is doing the action of our sentence, we need a verb ending to add to our verb base “niksIksuq”. We can use the “tuq” ending to tell us that “he” is fishing. You can read more about verb ending for statements here. 
        
      
    




    
      Niksiksullaturuq.

      
        Niksiksuq-llatu-ruq

        to.fish-to.enjoy-statement.he  

         This sentence has the same verb base from the previous line, “niksIksuq” which means to fish. 

         This time, we are going to add some extra information to the verb. Inupiaq can do this through what is called a “postbase”, which is always added after the verb base. This postbase, “llatu”, means “to enjoy”, so when added to our verb base: “niksIksuq” + “llatu”, it means “to enjoy fishing”. To make this a complete sentence, we still need to add a verb ending, which tells us who or what is doing the action.  

         Similar to the first line of the story, we can use the “tuq” ending to tell us that “he” enjoys fishing, but when the letter before the ending is a vowel, it changes to “ruq”. Since “llatu” ends with the vowel “u”, we use the ending “ruq” instead of “tuq” to mean “he” is the doer of the action. This chart can be a handy reference to find the correct verb ending for statements.

      
    




    
      Niksiksuqllatuviñ?

      
        Niksiksuq-llatu-viñ

        to.fish-to.enjoy-question.you

        This time we are asking a question instead of making a statement. We have the same information from the previous lines, such as the verb base “niksIksuq” and postbase “llatu”. The ending we add will help us say that we are asking a question and who we are asking the question about. To ask a question to “you”, we use the ending “viñ”. To see the whole chart of endings for questions, click here. 

      
    
  
  








  
  
    
      Aġnaġlu nukatpiaġlu kuvriqsuk.

      
        Agnaq-lu nukatpiaq-lu kuvrIq-tuk

        Postbase "lu" means "and". Notice it is marked on both subjects in the sentence.

        Ending "tuk" is for intransitive, indicative, third-person dual marking.

        Notice the strong i in "kuvrIq"? Near the end of the word, it palatalizes the "t" in "tuk" to "s".
      
    
    
    
      Nukatpiaq aquttuq.

      
        Nukatpiaq aqut-tuq

        Ending "tuq" is for intransitive, indicative, third-person singular. Note how it is different from "tuk" in the previous story line.
      
    
    
    
      Kuvriqsiḷḷaviñ?

      
        Kuvriq-si-ḷḷa-viñ

        Postbase "ḷḷa" means "to be able to".

        Ending "viñ" is for intransitive, interrogative, second-person, singular.
      
    
  
  







English


Let’s Read! by Edna Agheak MacLean


The boy is fishing.


He enjoys fishing.


Do you like fishing?



The woman and the young man are setting a net.


The young man is steering the boat.


Can you set a net?

title: Flip Book
About
text:
This is an online tool to learn more about the postbase system in Inupiaq while also engaging with Inupiat stories.
 How to use this tool 

This tool offers a way to read Inupiat stories online and interact with the structure of the language. This can help learners see how different elements of a word interact with each other in different ways.


There is an option to read each story in Inupiaq only, or Inupiaq and English. Additionally, if you hover your mouse over specific words, a pop-up bubble will offer information about the structure of the Inupiaq word and any additional or helpful notes.


Stems, or the base of a word, are colored green.


Postbases are colored magenta.


Endings, or inflections, are colored blue.


For linguists:

Please click on the “For linguists” tab. These stories will follow a similar format to the learner stories, but the information presented in the pop-up bubbles will instead include glosses and linguistic jargon.
 Postbase and word structure basics 

(information adapted from Myles Creed’s 2024 Ilisazaqta Inupiaqtun)

text:
Inupiaq





  
  
    
    
      Nukatpiaġruk  niksiksuqtuq.

      
        Nukatpiaġruk niksik-suq-tuq
        
         niksik means "to fish". It is the foundation for our Inupiaq word. 
        
         
        
      
    

    
      Niksiksullaturuq.

      
        Niksik-su-llatu-ruq.
        
         niksik means "to fish". It is the foundation for our Inupiaq sentence. 

         su means "regularly". 

         llatu means "to enjoy Xing".

         ruq is for sentences that are statements. It is also used when the subject of the sentence is "he/she/it".
      
    

    
      Niksiksullatuviñ?

      
        Niksik-su-llatu-viñ

        Ending "viñ" is for intransitive, interrogative, second-person singular.

        Ending "tuk" is for intransitive, indicative, third-person dual marking.

        Nukatpiaq aqut-tuq

        Ending "tuq" is for intransitive, indicative, third-person singular. Note how it is different from "tuk" in the previous story line.

title: Avinnaq by Arthur Douglas Sr.
text:
Inupiaq





  
  
    
    
      IỊaatnigguuq Aviññaq puuvruuraqtuq.
      
      
         IỊaatnigguuq Aviññaq puuvruu-raq-tuq. 
        
         Stem "puuvruu" means "to swim". 
        
         Ending "raq" is a past tense marker. 
        
         Ending "tuq" is for intransitive, indicative, third-person singular. Notice that "tuq" is used when following a consonant, and "ruq" is used when following a vowel.  
      
    
  





  
  
    
      lkaaġaa kuuk.
      
      
         lkaaq-ġaa kuuk. 
        
         Stem "ikaaq" means to cross. 
        
         Ending "ġaa" is for transitive, indicative verbs. Since both arguments (the subject and the object) are third-person, -a is added to +k/ga. 
        
      
    
  





  
  
    
      lkaaŋanikamiuŋguuqtai kiŋiaqhuni nipliqsuq,
      
      
         lkaaq-ŋanika-mi?-uŋguuqtai kiŋiaq-huni nipliq-suq, 
        
      
    
  





  
  
    
      "Kuukpaaluk ikaalla∤ualgitchiga kisima." 
      
      
         Kuuk-paaluk ikaa-lla∤ualgitchiga kisima. 
        
      
    
  





  
  
    
      Sunauvvagguuq uvva iñuum tutmavia maqatlami, imiġmik imalik ikaakkaŋa.
      
      
         Sunauvvagguuq uvva iñuum tutmi-avia maqatlami, imik-mik ima-lik ikaakkaŋa. 
        
      
    
  







English


 The Mouse Story by Arthur Douglas Sr. 


It is said that once upon a time, Mouse was swimming.


He crossed a river.


After he had crossed it, he looked back and proudly remarked,


“I have crossed the great big river all by myself.”


Actually, what had happened was that he had crossed a person’s footprint in soft mud which was filled with water.
